newsitem.title: CHILE: FEATURE - Chile banks merge to conquer Latin American markets.
newsitem.headline: FEATURE - Chile banks merge to conquer Latin American markets.

text.p: Faced with tough competition on their home turf, Chilean banks are merging to cut costs and become large enough to conquer far more lucrative markets in the rest of Latin America.

The first mega-banks have already emerged with the creation in January of Banco Santiago from the merger of Banco O'Higgins and Banco de Santiago and the takeover by Spain's Banco Santander SA of Banco Osorno.
Banks will be allowed to invest directly abroad this year once Congress passes a law easing tough restrictions imposed on the banking industry after the 1982 financial crisis.

But chafing at these curbs, bank owners have already formed financial groups which are making an aggressive lunge into markets from Argentina to Venezuela that offer faster growth than Chile's rapidly maturing economy.
"There is little new business in Chile and so banks must grow outside," said Susan McKenna, an analyst at brokers Celfin.
Expanding abroad has become pressing with banks facing a sharp profits squeeze as rising competition for their traditional customers bites into margins.

Government figures show that while loan portfolios swelled 12 percent last year, profits rose a scant three percent. These figures are before repayment of debt owed by private banks to the Central Bank.
ON THE HUNT FOR FOREIGN BUYS
Among Chile's most aggressive financiers is the Infisa group which, flush with cash from the sale of its stake in Banco Osorno, has recently snapped up banks in Peru and Venezuela.
Last month the group formed a pact with firms including Chase Manhattan to invest $750 million in financial companies throughout Latin America.
Also on the hunt for foreign buys is the Spanish-Chilean OHCH alliance, which owns Banco Santiago and has investments in four countries including Argentina and Paraguay.
The race is on to gain a foothold in other Latin American financial markets before the competition in these hots up too, said Rolando Jofre, second vice-president of Banco Santander.
"Other Latin American markets we are entering very strongly like Peru and Uruguay...are at this moment relatively uncompetitive," said Jofre.
"Given that they will become competitive, you have to move in fast. It's hard to catch up once you've been left behind."
BANKS LAG IN DASH ABROAD

The legal restrictions have meant that banks have lagged in the dash by Chilean firms to go abroad. Firms ranging from electricity utililities to pension funds have already spent billions of dollars this decade in investments throughout Latin America.
The new law will allow banks to buy stakes in foreign banks, set up branches abroad and make loans to Chilean clients operating oversees.

The bill was only given the green light by the government last year when Congress approved plans for private banks to repay billions of dollars of debt owed to the Central Bank which bailed them out during the 1982 crisis.

The law will not result in a stampede of banks rushing to expand abroad as many will have to merge to have the capital to make successful inroads into much larger markets like Argentina and Brazil, said Alejandro Alarcon, general manager of the Association of Banks and Financial Institutions.
"Banks will have to be significant in terms of assets to be able to compete abroad," said Alarcon.

The new law is still fairly restrictive and many banks will prefer to channel their foreign investments through financial companies like Infisa and OHCH to avoid restraints including checks from banking authorities, said McKenna.
"Most in management think it is easier to go abroad through holding companies as that avoids the superintendency," she said.
MERGER MANIA LOOMS

While long-awaited moves abroad may be slow to materialise, the domestic banking market will be shaken over coming years by a wave of mergers among medium-sized banks finding it hard to compete against giants like Santander and Santiago.
"The merger process will continue as it's difficult to be profitable with low volume," said Alarcon.
"Banks have to cut costs which is an incentive to merge."

Everyone agrees that with 33 private banks the market is crowded. Competition also comes from Chile's increasingly sophisticated capital markets which offer new, cheaper sources of finance to companies.
The number of niche banks is likely halve in coming years with firms like up-market Banco de A. Edwards and Banco Sud Americano are among the most sought takeover targets, analysts say.
Consolidation will come from mergers with other local banks or buyouts by foreigners like Spain's Banco Bilbao Vizcaya SA, which is believed to be hunting for deals in Chile.
"In the next three years, almost all niche banks will go through some sort of merger and acquisition transaction," said McKenna.
